## Abstract

The cell walls of rod-shaped Gram-positive bacteria are thick, multilayered networks that chirally twist as cells elongate. The underlying basis of twisting is not known, but probing the processes underlying this phenomenon may give insights into how cell wall material is inserted, how it evolves during cleavage, and the mechanics within the sacculus. In Bacillus subtilis, we see cell chains lacking hydrolases twist far slower than chains of wild-type cells, indicating that cell wall cleavage modulates the twisting rate. We see that when cells within chains separate, the two nascent ends rotate as they separate. Together, this suggests there is torsional stress within the cell wall that, when unreleased, perturbs overall chain morphology. Unlike Escherichia coli, we see that twisting does not arise from MreB's angle of motion, as its angle is identical in both fast-twisting wild-type cells and slow-twisting hydrolase-deficient cells. Rather, the circumferential insertion of glycans appears to establish this torsional stress, as increasing Rod complex activity by deleting ponA causes cells to twist faster than wild-type cells. Together, these experiments suggest the twisting of B. subtilis cells arises from radial glycan insertion, which somehow causes torsional stress in the wall that is later released by hydrolase activity.

## Abstract

Gram-positive rods like B. subtilis chirally twist as they grow, but the underlying basis for this phenomenon is unknown.

Using total internal reflection fluorescence and genetic manipulations, the authors measure the twist rate of cell chains as they modulate the number of hydrolases and Rod complex activity in the cell. This reveals changing how glycans are inserted and the number of hydrolase genes modulates twisting.

These experiments give new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the chiral twisting of B. subtilis, revealing the insertion of glycans somehow creates torsional stress in the wall that is later released by hydrolases, causing cells to twist.

## INTRODUCTION

Organisms across the domains of life protect themselves from the environment by building encapsulating cell walls, which also serve to retain the high cellular turgor to prevent lysis. For cells to grow, these rigid turgor-bearing cell walls must be modified to expand while maintaining their integrity. The proteins that synthesize and cleave the cell wall are mostly known in bacteria, but how this array of enzymes synergize to facilitate growth remains unclear.

One macroscopic phenomenon observed in rod-shaped bacteria is chiral twisting during growth: the ends of cells (or chains of cells) twist in opposite directions relative to each other. The processes underlying this emergent phenomenon remain unknown, but it is known that the amount of rotation is proportional to growth for a given strain and condition. For bacteria to grow, they must not only 1) add new material into the peptidoglycan (PG) meshwork, but they also must 2) cleave the PG meshwork so the cell wall can expand (Typas et al., 2011), and both processes have been implicated in chiral twisting during growth.

Two systems synthesize the glycans needed to elongate the PG cell wall for growth, each having opposing effects on rod shape: the class A PBPs and the Rod complex. The Rod complex inserts hoops of cell wall around the cell circumference, causing cells to elongate while maintaining their width (Domínguez-Escobar et al., 2011; Garner et al., 2011; van Teeffelen et al., 2011; Dion et al., 2019). Conversely, class A PBPs (aPBPs) are believed to fill in holes in the cell wall (Typas et al., 2011; Cho et al., 2016; Vigouroux et al., 2020), and aPBP activity does not appear oriented or constrained, causing cells to expand in all directions (Dion et al., 2019).

The elongation of Bacillus subtilis cells is driven by internal turgor (Rojas et al., 2017). However, elongation of these pressurized cells is limited by cleavage of the cell wall (Fan and Beckman, 1971; Meisner et al., 2013), a process conducted by enzymes called hydrolases. Different hydrolase families cleave different chemical bonds within the PG network, and some are involved in cleaving the sidewall PG, while others cleave septal PG to facilitate cell separation (Vollmer et al., 2008).

Two general models have been proposed for how bacteria twist, each arising from observations in two bacterial model organisms, Escherichia coli and B. subtilis. The more recent model, built from observations in E. coli, posed the rate of twisting was determined by the amount of skew in the angle of MreB filaments relative to the cell's short axis. The twisting rate changed with different MreB mutants or when PBP2 was replaced with PBP2s from other organisms. In both experiments, cell twist correlated with the angle of MreB filaments or their motion (Wang et al., 2012; Tropini et al., 2014). Likewise, beads fixed to E. coli rotated during osmotic shocks, and the left-handed chirality of MreB spirals correlated with and was required for left-handed twisting during growth (Wang et al., 2012). Overall, this model proposes that the angle of MreB filaments causes the insertion of angled glycans into the wall, thus determining the rate of cell twisting. This model is similar to the “helical insertion” of cell wall proposed by Mendelson to explain the twisting of B. subtilis macrofibers (Mendelson, 1990), long bundles (100’s of cells thick) of chained cells that are visible to the naked eye.

However, in B. subtilis, MreB filament angle is unlikely to be involved in cell twisting, as MreB filaments (and all other Rod complex components) show no skew in their angle of motion (Domínguez-Escobar et al., 2011; Garner et al., 2011; Hussain et al., 2018). Similarly, twisting can also be changed or reversed by the addition of cycloserine or D-alanine (Mendelson and Karamata, 1982; Mendelson, 1988; Surana et al., 1988) both of which affect glycan cross-linking (Kuru et al., 2012), suggesting glycan insertion and/or cross-linking is somehow involved in modulating the twist rate and chirality.

Another model for both the growth and twisting of Bacillus cells is the “surface stress model” proposed by Koch (Koch, 2001). This model is based on multiple observations and assumptions: 1) Turgor pressure drives the elongation of rod-shaped cells (Rojas et al., 2017). 2) New cell wall material is inserted at the bottom of the wall closest to the membrane and moves upward as new PG is added beneath it (Koch and Doyle, 1985) until it is shed off of the cell wall surface. 3) Glycans are inserted diffusively along the cell length, and the walls of a rod under pressure have greater stresses in the axial direction compared with the longitudinal axis. 4) The observation that hydrolysis-deficient B. subtilis cells formed macrofibers, long bundles of chained cells that are hundreds of cells thick. It was found that adding lysozyme to macrofibres with limited hydrolysis activity caused them to “relax” from a highly twisted state to a less twisted state (Mendelson et al., 1984; Favre et al., 1986).

In Koch's surface stress model for bacterial growth, roughly circumferentially oriented glycans are inserted and cross-linked into the wall at the bottom layer of the wall closest to the cell membrane. These glycans move upward due to new glycans being inserted underneath them, causing them to become increasingly stressed as they move outward due to increasing radius (Koch and Doyle, 1985). Overall, the inner wall layers bear the dominant circumferential stress from turgor pressure, whereas the outer layers are under more axial stress because they accommodate elongation (Koch, 1989, 2001). At the point where the cell wall is most axial stressed in the axial direction, the cross-links are then cleaved by stress-sensing hydrolases, allowing the sacculus to expand longitudinally (Koch et al., 1982; Koch, 1983, 1989; Koch, 1990).

Koch further proposed that cell twisting during growth arises from differences in the stresses on glycans in the axial and longitudinal directions. Cracks should form in the direction of maximum stress, ideally causing longitudinal (aka axial) cracks to form due to the dominant hoop stress. However, Koch suggested that the outer, fragmented layers redistribute stresses in a way that deviates from purely axial or circumferential directions. This modification of stress patterns would cause 1) cracks to at an angle that then propagate around the cell in a spiral, causing cells to twist, and 2) cracks that propagate downward as lower layers are become under stress, allowing the twist to continue as the cells grow (Koch, 1989). However, spiral cracks on the surface have not yet been observed by electron microscopy (EM) or atomic force microscopy (AFM). Furthermore, this model does not explain why such “spiral cracks” could have a range of different—yet reproducible—handedness and twist rates in different strains under defined conditions.

As our knowledge of the identity and function of the proteins involved in cell growth has improved, as have our tools to genetically manipulate and assay single B. subtilis cells, we wished to reexamine how cell wall synthesis and hydrolysis affect the twisting of B. subtilis. Furthermore, we wanted to explore B. subtilis twisting by examining single chains of cells rather than the large macrofiber bundles composed of hundreds of cells, as done previously.

## RESULTS

To explore how 1) PG insertion and 2) PG hydrolysis are involved in B. subtilis twisting, we first attempted to deconvolute these two activities by assaying twisting rates in wild-type cells and cells with minimal hydrolase activity. For this, we used our “∆40” strain (Wilson et al., 2023), where we removed nearly all the hydrolyses, leaving the two synthetically lethal hydrolases cwlO and lytE (Hashimoto et al., 2012; Meisner et al., 2013). To measure the rate B. subtilis cells twist, we adapted an assay developed to study E. coli twisting (Tropini et al., 2014), but rather than labeling the cell wall with fluorescent Wheat Germ Agglutinin, we labeled the wall with fluorescent D-amino acids (FDAAs), which covalently cross-link into the cell wall. We created AlexaFluor488-DAA carboxamides that incorporate into the cell wall as it is synthesized (Kuru et al., 2012) in the carboxamide form, which prevents them from being cleaved off the muropeptide by carboxypeptidases (Lebar et al., 2014). For our assay, we grew cells in 20 µM FDAAs for 1.5 h, then placed the cells under an agar pad on a coverslip. We then used total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) illumination microscopy to bleach the FDAA signal on the bottom side of cells and subsequently acquired timelapses to observe the fluorescence recovery from the unbleached top portion of the cell chain as it rotated into the TIRF illumination plane. The amount of rotation averaged from both ends after a given amount of growth is the twisting rate, that is, the amount of rotation per amount of growth.

With our assay established, we first tested whether hydrolases could affect twisting in B. subtilis, comparing the twisting rates of wild-type (PY79) cells to ∆40 cells. These assays revealed the ∆40 strain has a slower twisting rate relative to wild-type cells. In wild-type cells, recovery of FDAA fluorescence first occurred at the ends and chirally (left-handed) propagated inward, with recovery becoming visible near the middle of the chain within one doubling of length (Figure 1A top left; Supplemental Movie S1). In contrast, the ∆40 strain twisted far less over the same interval: cells showed a substantially reduced recovery, with only a relatively small portion recovering fluorescence at the ends and no recovery propagating to the middle over the same period (Figure 1A top middle; Supplemental Movie S2). Notably ∆40 cells twisted predominantly left-handed, but some twisted right-handed. Kymographs drawn from the cell poles along the midline further demonstrated the ∆40 strain had a substantially reduced twisting rate (Figure 1A bottom).

To quantify the differences in twisting rates, we measured the fluorescence recovery from both ends as a function of growth: we plotted the fluorescence recovery from both ends of the cell chain at each timepoint against how much the cells had increased in length from the initial timepoint. We corrected the signal at each point for cell wall turnover; rates measured by quantitating the rate of fluorescence loss in unbleached cells (Supplemental Figure S1A). Notably, the rates of fluorescence decrease in wild-type cells matched past measurements of cell wall turnover measured with radiolabeled N-Acetylglucosamine (Blackman et al., 1998), indicating photobleaching was negligible. We assayed cell chains > 300 pixels (19 µm) in length, as wild-type cell chains shorter than this showed erratic twisting behaviors (Supplemental Figure S1B). To compare signals between cells, we normalized the intensity of each frame between zero and one, with one being the intensity of the frame right before bleaching and zero being the frame immediately after bleaching (Supplemental Figure S1B). This revealed that the ∆40 strain showed a much slower rate of fluorescence recovery (t25%, the amount of growth to achieve 25% recovery = 58 µM) compared with wild-type cells (t25% = 7.5 µM) (Figure 1, A and B; Supplemental Figure S1C). To further test hydrolase activity for twisting, we examined twisting rates in wild-type cells with only lytC and lytD removed, the two hydrolases responsible for cell wall turnover (Blackman et al., 1998). ∆lytC ∆lytD cells (left-handed twist) showed more fluorescence recovery than ∆40 cells but less than wild-type cells over the same amount of growth (t25% = 12 µM) (Figure 1, A and B; Supplemental Figure S1C; Supplemental Movie S3). To gain a more exact estimate of the rates of recovery per cell length change (%Recovery/∆µM). For this, we attained the slope of the first six points after bleaching; as beyond this point, the slope of wild-type cells became less linear, likely due to the bleached portion re-entering the TIRF field of view. This gave an average twisting rate of 0.03835 (%Recovery/∆µM) for wild-type cells, 0.00332 (%Recovery/∆µM) for the ∆40 strain (PY79 vs. ∆40 p-value < 0.0001), and 0.00413 (%Recovery/∆µM) for ∆lytC ∆lytD cells (PY79 and ∆40 vs ∆lytC ∆lytD p-value <0.0001) (Supplemental Figure S1, D and E). Together, these experiments demonstrate that increased hydrolase activity increases the rate of cell twisting, suggesting there may be torsional strain in the wall, a strain that is released by hydrolases cleaving glycans or their peptide cross-links.

As noted above, Koch proposed that cell twisting arose from the appearance and propagation of spiral cracks around the bacteria (Koch, 1989). During unrelated experiments in the Physiology course at Marine Biological Labs, we conducted expansion microscopy of FDAA-labeled B. subtills cells without digesting the cell wall prior to expansion. This resulted in sacculi being stretched by expansion, causing many of them to fracture. These fractures occurred either perpendicularly to the cell's long axis or—similar to Koch's predictions—in a spiral pattern wrapping around the cell length (Figure 1C).

Unlike E. coli, in B. subtilis, the separation of cells occurs after the division septum has been completed, and cells in rich media grow as long chains of individual cells. While observing twisting in various strains, we noticed that upon cell separation, the nascent cell ends exhibited a rapid recovery of fluorescence (relative to the twisting occurring during growth) (Figure 2A; Supplemental Movies S4 and S5). Further evidence for twisting during separation arose from AFM studies of B. subtills cells, where we observed a spiral organization of cell wall material connecting two cells undergoing separation (Figure 2B). Accordingly, wild-type cells, which contain the hydrolases facilitating cell separation, twist and separate more cleanly and gradually than ∆40 cells, while ∆40 cells suddenly finish separating and rapidly twist. Furthermore, separating ∆40 cell ends often twisted more upon separation than wild-type cells (Figure 2A). Further evidence for twisting during separation arose from AFM studies of B. subtills cells, where we observed a spiral organization of cell wall material connecting two cells undergoing separation (Figure 2B). This twisting during separation further demonstrates that the cell wall is under torsional stress, stress that is released by cell separation hydrolases. A physical analogy for this behavior is that separating cells twist in a similar manner as an elastic string that is wound, and when cut, the two newly created ends twist chirally. This torsional stress is likely also gradually released by the growth hydrolases during cell elongation, causing growth-mediated cell twisting, in line with previous observations and models from macrofiber studies (Koch, 1989, 2001).

We next examined the effect of septa on cell twisting. Our initial experiments measured twisting in B. subtilis chains made of multiple cells connected by division septa (Figure 1A). To examine how the presence or absence of septa affected twisting, we blocked the formation of division septa by expressing MciZ, a protein that depolymerizes FtsZ filaments (Bisson-Filho et al., 2015). Wild-type cells with septa showed similar twisting relative to cells lacking septa via MciZ expression (wild-type cells = 0.03835 (%recovery/∆µM), PY79 + MciZ = 0.03337 (%recovery/∆µM), (P-value = 0.1991) (Figure 2C; Supplemental Figure S2, A, B, and E). Likewise, there was no significant difference in the average twisting rate of ∆40 cells with or without MciZ (∆40 = 0.00332(%recovery/∆µM), ∆40 + MciZ = 0.004129 (%recovery/∆µM) (P-value = 0.6219) (Figure 2C; Supplemental Figure S2, C–E). All above strains twisted left-handed. Combined with the above observations (Figure 2, A and B), these experiments suggest 1) twisting during growth occurs via the addition of cell wall used for cell elongation and not division, and 2) rapid twisting of cells occurs only when cell separation, not from the formation or presence of division septa. However, we occasionally observed instances, especially in ∆40 cells, where cell separation appears often incomplete, where the twisting appeared to be reduced or blocked at septa where cells have not completed separation (Figure 2E), which may arise from loosely connected, and no longer stress-bearing, material connecting the chains.

Next, we examined the role of the MreB filaments and the associated Rod complex in cell twisting. Previous work found that in E. coli, the skew in the angle or motion of MreB filaments to the cell's short axis correlated with E. coli’s twisting rate (Wang et al., 2012; Tropini et al., 2014). However, B. subtilis MreB filaments have not been seen to have any skew in their angle or motion (Domínguez-Escobar et al., 2011; Garner et al., 2011). To examine whether MreB's angle of motion correlated with cell twist in B. subtilis, we examined MreB motion in both the ∆40 strain and wild-type cells as they exhibit very different twist rates. For this, we created strains where MreB was fused to HaloTag at the native locus in both wild-type and ∆40 cells, sparsely labeled MreB with JF594-Halo ligand, then tracked the motions of single molecules of MreB using TIRF. This revealed that, despite having dramatically different twisting rates, the angular distributions of MreB motion were identical between wild-type and ∆40 cells (P = 0.699) (Figure 3A). This demonstrates that in B. subtilis, the twisting rates and angle of MreB motion are independent of each other.

The rapid twisting of cells suggests hydrolases release torsional stress stored within the wall, but in the absence of chiral (off-axis) glycan insertion, what processes cause this stress to arise? Past work has shown B. subtilis twisting can be changed or reversed by the addition of D-alanine (Mendelson, 1988), which competes with muropeptide cross-linking (Kuru et al., 2012). Likewise, replacing the transpeptidase in the Rod complex (PBP2) with PBP2s from other organisms changes E. coli's twisting rate (Tropini et al., 2014). Past work has shown B. subtilis twisting can be changed or reversed by the addition of D-alanine (Mendelson, 1988), which competes with muropeptide cross-linking (Kuru et al., 2012). Thus, it could be that Rod complex activity, or glycan insertion in general, is somehow involved in creating (or modulating) these emergent stresses.

To test this, we modulated the relative amount of oriented versus unoriented glycans in the wall. Our previous work found all the PG synthesis used for cell elongation comes from two enzymatic systems with opposite effects on cell shape: the Rod complex inserts circumferential material, decreasing rod width, while class A PBPs insert unoriented material, increasing rod width (Dion et al., 2019). Furthermore, when the activity of one system was reduced, the activity of the other system increased, presumably due to a shift in the relative utilization of the shared cell wall precursor Lipid II (Dion et al., 2019). We wanted to assay how increased Rod complex activity affected cell twisting, but increasing Rod complex activity by overexpressing mreBCD only slightly thins cells (754 nm → 697 nm) while removing the major class A PBP ponA has a substantial effect on cell width (754 nm → 581 nm) as all the PG used for growth is inserted by the Rod complex (Dion et al., 2019). Thus, to examine whether Rod complex activity had any effect on cell twisting, we examined the twisting rate of ∆ponA cells. However, ∆ponA cells are kinked and do not lay flat, causing uneven bleaching and thus inhibiting our twisting assay. When MciZ was expressed in ∆ponA cells, cells were mostly flat and could be more successfully assayed. Movies and kymographs revealed ∆ponA MciZ expressing cells twist (left-handed) much faster than wild-type cells, undergoing at least one full revolutions, while wild-type cells had not completed one revolution within the same period (Figure 3B; Supplemental Figure S3A). Quantitating these rates verified that ∆ponA cells twist dramatically faster than wild-type cells expressing MciZ (∆ponA t25% = ∼3.6 µM vs. t25% of PY79 = ∼8.5 µM for wild-type), and recovery rates calculated from single cells’ linear estimate slopes were 0.1027 (%recovery/∆µM) for ∆ponA and 0.3337% recovery/∆µM for wild-type (P-value <0.0001) (Supplemental Figure S3, B and C; Supplemental Movies S6 and S7). Notably, our ∆ponA twisting rate is likely an underestimate, as ∆ponA cells already begun twisting in between the bleaching step and the first image acquisition. These experiments show that increasing Rod complex activity increases twist rate, in line with a model that PG insertion by the Rod complex establishes torsional stress in the cell wall.

Across our strains, we observed different overall chain morphologies associated with each strain's twist rate: cells containing reduced hydrolases that have reduced twisting rates are less straight (Figure 3, A–C). Rod complex activity also affected chain morphology: deleting ponA in ∆40 cells caused chains to become extremely supercoiled (Figure 3D). Given the contiguous cell wall determines the overall chain shape, in light of our prior observations, this suggests that the more unreleased torsional stress that exists in the wall, the more the chain begins to buckle and writhe, and in the most extreme cases, supercoil upon themselves; a macroscopic physical analogy for these extreme cases would be how elastic strings begin to supercoil as the ends are continually twisted.

## DISCUSSION

The above experiments examining B. subtilis twisting during its growth indicate there is a torsional stress in the cell wall. This stress increases as we change the relative fraction of circumferentially oriented glycans (made by the Rod complex) to unoriented glycans (made by class A PBPs) in the wall. Subsequently, torsional stress is released by hydrolases breaking bonds in the cell wall, causing cells to twist as they elongate and separate. The more circumferential glycans, the more torsional stress, and the more hydrolase activity, the more stress is released. As the accumulation of torsional stress and the release of stress becomes more imbalanced, cell chains increasingly show more kinking and supercoiling, a behavior consistent with materials containing increased amounts of unreleased torsional stress.

Our wild-type B. subtilis strain twists 2x slower than MG1655 E. coli (Tropini et al., 2014), and just like E. coli, all our B. subtilis strains twist left-handed under our growth conditions, except for ∆40, which occasionally also twists right, being closer to the inversion point where cells switch their twist chirality. However, in contrast to E. coli (Wang et al., 2012; Tropini et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2020), we see no correlation between twisting rate and MreB's angle of motion. Thus, B. subtilis twisting is unlikely to arise from helical insertion, as proposed by Mendelson (Mendelson, 1990), or an angle of (or twist within) MreB filaments, as has been proposed to underly E. coli twisting (Wang et al., 2012; Tropini et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2020).

If glycan insertion is not chiral in B subtilis, what processes give rise to torsional stress and emergent twisting? This is a difficult question, as chirality could arise from—or be affected by—many different sources. Given that there is no observable chirality in the insertion of glycans, one simple possibility is that B. subtilis twisting arises emergently due to spontaneous symmetry breaking if symmetric nontwisting cell growth is unstable, a spontaneous symmetry breaking akin to what is seen in whirlpools and tornados (Shtern and Hussain, 1999). This could include an emergent chirality of glycans arising from nonchiral glycans (circumferentially oriented) that occurs during the evolution of glycans as they move from the membrane outward through the cell wall. Indeed, Koch's model for how twisting arising from nonchiral glycans invokes such a symmetry breaking: He proposed twisting arises due to 1) differences in the stresses on glycans in the axial and longitudinal directions and 2) that the outer, fragmented layers redistribute stress in a way that deviates from being purely axial or circumferential, thereby causing cracks to spontaneously occur at an angle, which then self-propagate both in a spiral around the cell as well as into lower layers of the wall, thereby propagating chirality as cells grow (Koch, 1989).

Regardless if spontaneous symmetry breaking is involved, as the chirality and twist rate of a given strain 1) is reproducible in given growth conditions, and 2) can be reproducibly modulated with genetic or external perturbations, it is evident the magnitude and direction of torsional strain is likely somehow determined by how glycans are inserted into the wall and/or their subsequent evolution as they move upward through the cell wall layers. For example, even though glycans inserted by the Rod complex are not chiral, aspects of their insertion modulate twisting: the rate and/or handedness of B. subtilis twist can be changed by both the amount of Rod complex activity (found here), exogenous D-amino acids, and compounds that inhibit muropeptide cross-linking (Mendelson and Karamata, 1982; Mendelson, 1988; Surana et al., 1988). Thus, it may be that torsional stress and chirality arise from the fraction of 1) circumferentially oriented versus unoriented glycans in the wall and/or 2) their amount of cross-linking to each other. However, twist handedness and rate can also be changed by (among other perturbations) temperature, media composition, and magnesium, so it may be that other biochemical or mechanical features also play a role.

These experiments reveal that the wall contains torsional strain is built up in the wall somewhere between the insertion of glycans and their cleavage, but deconvoluting the molecular and mechanical aspects that determine twist handedness and rate poses a future challenge given the complex multilayered and evolving nature of the cell wall. An examination of how glycans are arranged in different layers of the wall with AFM or Cryo-focused ion beam EM might shed insight into this phenomenon. Direct measurements of forces within the wall and its different layers would be most informative, but this presents extreme experimental challenges. However, computational modeling may provide further insights and constraints into how the macroscopic behavior of B. subtilis twisting arises from the formation, stretching, and breaking of bonds within the multilayered cell wall.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

Request a protocol through Bio-protocol

### Growth

Strains are stored in glycerol at –80°C and, the day prior to an experiment, are streaked on an LB plate and grown overnight at 37°C. On the morning of an experiment, a single colony is picked off the LB plate and grown in 1 ml prewarmed to 37°C casein hydrolysate (CH) media and grown on a roller at 37°C for around 2 h, or until OD600 is ∼0.2. Cells were then diluted 1:20 and grown for another 30 min. When the OD600 neared 0.05, 160 µl of culture was then added to 16 µl of 200 uM FDA stain.

### Microscopy

TIRFM and brightfield were performed using a Nikon Eclipse SIM-S system equipped with an SR HP Apo TIRF 100xH objective, a Hamamatsu Flash4.0 sCMOS camera, and a Nikon LUNV laser module containing both 488 and 561 laser lines. The acquisition software was Nikon Elements 5.21.0.1. Cultures were grown to an OD600 below 0.3. 1.5 µl of cell culture was then placed under a prewarmed 2% agarose pad containing growth medium inside a prewarmed 60 mM MatTek #1.5 glass bottom dish. The dishes were then placed in the 37 °C incubator chamber on the microscope and allowed to thermally equilibrate for 15 min.

### Microscopy for cell twisting

Our assay is adapted from the “Twist n’ TIRF” assay from Tropini et al. used to study E. coli twisting (Tropini et al., 2014). After growth, the cell wall of strains were fully labeled by growing them in media containing 20 µm AlexaFlour488-DAA carboxamide (Wuxi AppTech) for ∼1.5 h (at least 1 h, or 2 generations to reach maximum staining, data not shown). This FDAA concentration is 10x less than concentrations that affect growth.

Optimal fields of view were found by scanning in brightfield for chains of cells that would fit in the field of view after a doubling in length. An initial brightfield and TIRF image was acquired before bleaching. Total internal reflection illumination with a 488 laser (40%, no ND filter) with total internal reflection was used to bleach the bottom side of the FDAA-labeled cells (4 s exposure). After bleaching the bottom side of cells, TIRF images were acquired with the 488 laser at reduced power (50% power with an ND8 filter) every 1.5 min (4-s exposures), alongside brightfield images with a 0.7 µm shift in the Z-plane relative to TIRF focus. All timelapses were at least 1 h long. Controls (equivalent imaging of dead FDAA-labeled cells) were conducted to ensure that photobleaching was negligible over the imaging interval and illumination conditions.

### Twisting analysis

To quantify cell twisting, the sum of fluorescence within cell contours was measured after background subtraction (rolling ball with 250 radius). Cell outlines were segmented with a simple threshold using the mean of the histograms stacked from the timelapse. Manual selection was used to select the binary segmented images for each cell for each frame in the timelapse. Importantly, only nonseparating chains of cells were used for measurements; once a chain separated, it was no longer considered. As small cells (< 300 pixels) showed random and instantaneous recoveries of FDAA fluorescence (perhaps due to rolling), only cell chains with > 300 pixels in length in the first frame were considered for analysis.

The fluorescent FDAA signal was subsequently corrected for cell wall turnover that occurs during cell growth, a rate measured by calculating the fluorescent decrease of unbleached FDAA-labeled cells during their growth with the TIRF assay. These measures matched previous measures of cell wall turnover of B. subtilis assayed using radiolabeled glucosamine (Pooley, 1976; Wilson et al., 2023).

All twist recovery data in figures are shown as MIN/MAX Normalized total signal plotted versus the change in cell length relative to the initial cell length. The first frame (before bleaching) is the brightest (MAX), and the second frame is the darkest (MIN). Notably, as twisting is relevant to the amount of growth that occurs, normalized fluorescence is plotted with respect to the absolute change in length from the initial timepoint, thereby normalizing the twist across chains of various lengths. “Twisting rates” reported in the text were calculated by linear regression fits for the first few points (points 3 to 8 following bleaching) for all data and taking the mean of these slopes.

### Microscopy for MreB angle of motion

Following growth in CH as outlined above, MreB-Halotag inside cells were stained with a final concentration of 0.5–3 nM JF549 for 20 min before being placed under an agar pad on a bottom Matek dish. Bright-field images were initially acquired for cell outlines and midlines. Fluorescent images with 561 nm exposure were acquired with 300 ms exposure every 1 s.

### Methods for analysis of MreB movement relative to the cell midline

Briefly, the thresholding of brightfield images was conducted using the threshold function FIJI. Next, the cell contours and midline of each cell were calculated based on the segmentation mask of the bright field image using Morphometrics.

Particle tracking of MreB-HaloTag was performed using FIJI and the TrackMate plugin (Tinevez et al., 2017). Spots with a diameter of 250 nm were identified using the Laplacian of Gaussians (LoG) detector. These spots were tracked over a 150 nm search radius using the linear motion LAP tracker in TrackMate. No missing links or gaps were allowed. Only tracks that are longer than six frames were used for calculations of particle velocity. Tracks were excluded if the R-squared for the linear fitting of tracks was less than 0.85. Single-molecule trajectories were discarded if displacement was < 150 nm. We calculated the mean track position to determine whether a track is within a cell contour. The point of intersection between the linear fit of the track and midline was then calculated, and the point of intersection of the midline and the two points next to it were used for the linear fit of the midline. The angle between the track and the cell midline was then calculated from the line of best fit. The range of angles is between 0 and 180. All analyses were performed using custom MATLAB code.

### Expansion microscopy of HADA-labeled cells

A single colony of bGL19 (dacA::Kan) cells were picked off the LB plate and grown in 1 ml prewarmed to 37°C CH media and grown on a roller at 37°C for 1 h. Next, HADA-FDAA was added to the culture tube to a final concentration of 2 mM, and cells were grown for 2 h. Cells were concentrated by centrifugation and fixed and expanded with only one round of expansion, as described previously (Tillberg et al., 2016; Asano et al., 2018). Importantly, the cell wall was not digested with lysozyme prior to expansion.

### AFM for septa during separation

B. subtilis cells at midexponential phase were boiled rapidly to kill bacterial cells and inactivate any potential hydrolase activity. Cells were broken by French Press and FastPrep, then suspended in 5% (wt/vol) SDS and boiled for 25 min, and sacculi were collected by centrifugation at 20,000 × g for 3 min. The resulting pellets were washed with distilled water to remove all traces of SDS, then resuspended in Tris-HCl (50 mM, pH 7) containing 2 mg/ml pronase and incubated at 60°C for 90 min. The resulting sacculi were then resuspended in LC-MS Chromasolv water for storage at −20°C.

Freshly cleaved mica discs were incubated with Cell-Tak {285 ml of 100 mM NaHCO3 (pH 8), then 10 µl of Cell-Tak [Corning, 5% (wt/vol) in acetic acid] and 5 µl of 1 M NaOH, covered and left for 20 min then washed five times with high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) grade water} to ensure the attachment of sacculi on the glass surface. Sacculi were diluted in HPLC-grade water to the appropriate concentration and dried onto mica using N2. These were further washed and dried with N2 again to remove any unattached samples.

All AFM data were taken on a JPK Nanowizard III in quantitative imaging mode. Samples were imaged in HPLC Grade water using a FastScanD cantilever (Bruker, Santa Barbara), nominal spring constant 0.25 N/m with a 256 × 256-pixel scan region, driven at ∼167 Hz with a typical Z length of ∼300 nm using peak interaction forces of 2–3 nN. Images were flattened to a median of differences and first-order planefit using Gwyddion.

### Statistics

For all boxplots throughout this work, boxes indicate the 25th–75th percentiles, whiskers indicate the 1.5x interquartile range, the midline of the box indicates the median, and + indicates the mean. For all other graphs, error bars represent SD. For envelope plots, the thick line is the mean, and the top and bottom dashed curves represent ±1 SD. The number of samples and experimental replicates is detailed in “Data numbers and experimental trials.” P values were calculated in GraphPad Prism 10 using a two-tailed Mann–Whitney test. Mann–Whitney was used as the data were not Gaussian distributed.

## Abstract

Background: Chagas disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, remains a major public health problem in Latin America and an emerging concern worldwide. Current chemotherapies show limited efficacy during chronic infection, and no licensed vaccine is currently available. We previously developed the chimeric antigen N-Tc52/TSKb20 as a vaccine candidate against T. cruzi infection. In a murine model, this vaccine induced robust antigen-specific immune response associated with protection shortly after vaccination. Objectives: Here, we investigated the long-term persistence and effector functions of the immune responses elicited by this vaccine candidate. Methods: Both female and male C57BL/6 mice were immunized with three doses of N-Tc52/TSKb20 formulated with QuilA adjuvant. Serum samples collected 170 days post-immunization were analyzed for antigen-specific antibodies by ELISA and for trypanolytic activity against cell-derived trypomastigotes using an in vitro functional assay. Cellular immune responses were evaluated by measuring cytokine production, T cell activation, and memory T cell responses following in vitro re-stimulation with the vaccine antigen or T. cruzi antigens. Results: N-Tc52/TSKb20 vaccination induced a sustained antigen-specific humoral response, characterized by long-lasting IgG2c antibodies and functional activity persisting for up to 170 days post-immunization. In parallel, vaccination promoted long-term activation of antigen-specific CD8+ T cells and production of TNF-α and IFN-γ upon antigen re-encounter. A sex-dependent tendency was observed for IL-10, with increased production in vaccinated female mice. Moreover, vaccinated animals exhibited increased frequencies of central and effector memory CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in response to T. cruzi antigens, with a predominant contribution of CD8+ T cells, indicating the establishment of parasite-specific T cell memory. Conclusions: Together, these findings demonstrate that vaccination with N-Tc52/TSKb20 induces a long-lasting Th1-biased immune response characterized by trypanolytic antibodies, functional and durable T cell responses, and parasite-specific memory T cells. This immunological profile supports the potential of N-Tc52/TSKb20 as a promising vaccine candidate for Chagas disease and highlights its capacity to elicit immune mechanisms that have been associated with protection against T. cruzi infection.

## 1. Introduction

Vaccination remains one of the most powerful tools in public health, preventing millions of deaths each year by priming the immune system to recognize and eliminate pathogens before disease onset [1]. However, the true success of vaccination depends not only on the magnitude of the initial immune response but also on its durability. Long-lasting immune protection, mediated by long-lived plasma cells, memory B cells, and memory T lymphocytes, enables the immune system to mount rapid and effective effector responses upon pathogen encounter without the need for frequent booster doses [2,3]. These durable responses are critical for vaccine effectiveness, as they allow early control of infection, thereby preventing severe disease, reducing morbidity and mortality, and limiting pathogen transmission [4,5].

Licensed human vaccines confer varying degrees of long-term protection. While some provide lifelong immunity, others require booster doses at defined intervals, and some must be administered annually [5]. This variability in the durability of vaccine-induced protection underscores the importance of evaluating the persistence of immune responses as a formulation-dependent feature. Despite its relevance, the mechanisms underlying long-term immunity following vaccination remain incompletely understood [3]. In this context, many infectious diseases caused by microorganisms still lack a licensed vaccine. Chagas disease (CD), caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi (T. cruzi), is one such example. CD remains one of the most neglected tropical diseases, silently affecting more than six million people worldwide. Originally confined to Latin America, it is increasingly emerging beyond endemic regions as a consequence of global migration, with transmission now occurring predominantly through non-vectorial routes such as vertical infection, blood transfusion, and organ transplantation [6,7,8]. T. cruzi infection represents a complex immunological challenge: the parasite exhibits remarkable antigenic diversity, persistence strategies and immune evasion mechanisms that subvert both innate and adaptive immune responses, resulting in a delicate balance between parasite control and tissue damage [9,10]. Additionally, the limited understanding of the pathophysiology of CD and the complex host–parasite interactions continue to hinder the development of an effective vaccine against T. cruzi [11]. Various vaccine strategies have been explored, ranging from early approaches based on inactivated or attenuated parasites to the evaluation of purified parasite antigens [12,13,14,15,16,17,18]. More recently, recombinant proteins and subunit vaccines have emerge as promising alternatives [19,20,21,22,23,24,25]. Current vaccine design increasingly focuses on incorporating multiple epitopes that target distinct immune pathways, aiming to enhance both the breadth and magnitude of the protective immune response [26,27,28,29,30]. The outcomes and limitations of these different approaches have been extensively reviewed elsewhere [11,31,32,33,34].

In the development of vaccines against T. cruzi, protective immune responses must persist long after immunization to ensure rapid control of parasite infection [35]. To date, no validated correlates of protection reliably predict vaccine efficacy against CD [36,37,38]. However, studies in experimental models and infected individuals have identified key immune mechanisms involved in parasite control, particularly cellular responses associated with protection against intracellular pathogens [39]. Although these responses are widely used as reference parameters to evaluate candidate vaccines, they do not constitute definitive predictors of efficacy. In this context, the induction and maintenance of durable immune memory emerge as fundamental features of effective vaccination [40,41]. Therefore, assessing the persistence of immune responses associated with protection represents a critical component in the development and evaluation of vaccine strategies against T. cruzi.

Recent work from our group has provided compelling evidence that the rational combination of immunodominant parasite domains within a recombinant chimeric protein represents a powerful strategy to enhance immunogenicity and protective efficacy [42]. Among the selected components of our recombinant chimera is the amino-terminal domain of the T. cruzi Tc52 protein, which has been shown to induce functional antibodies associated with partial protection against infection [20]. The second component is TSKb20, an immunodominant CD8+ T cell epitope derived from the Trans-sialidase family, whose antigen-specific cellular responses have also been associated with protection in experimental models [43]. Vaccination with the N-Tc52/TSKb20 chimera previously demonstrated the ability to elicit robust and coordinated humoral and cellular immune responses shortly after immunization. These responses were characterized by the induction of IgG2c antibodies and the activation of TSKb20-specific CD8+ T cells and were associated with effective control of T. cruzi infection following challenge, resulting in superior protection compared with either antigenic domain alone [42]. Collectively, these findings highlight the potential of N-Tc52/TSKb20 to drive functional and protective immunity against T. cruzi.

In the present study, we sought to define the durability and functional capacity of the immune responses elicited by the N-Tc52/TSKb20 antigen 170 days after the last immunization, focusing on immunological memory as a hallmark of effective vaccination. We performed a comprehensive evaluation of both humoral and cellular responses in a C57BL/6 murine model at approximately six months after the final immunization. Given the dual extracellular and intracellular nature of T. cruzi, this integrated approach enabled the characterization of immune mechanisms required for sustained parasite control. Altogether, these analyses provide critical insights into the longevity and functional competence of the immune response induced by the N-Tc52/TSKb20 chimera, further reinforcing its potential as a promising vaccine candidate against CD.

## 2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. Animal Model

C57BL/6 female and male mice (8 weeks old) were used throughout these experiments. Animals were housed in groups of up to five per cage under controlled temperature (25 °C) and a 12 h light/12 h dark photoperiod, with ad libitum access to standard feed and water. At the end of the experiments, animals were euthanized by controlled carbon dioxide (CO2) exposure to minimize suffering. Animal breeding and experimental procedures were conducted at the Animal Facility of the Instituto de Patología Experimental, Universidad Nacional de Salta, Argentina. All procedures were reviewed and approved by the Comité Institucional para el Cuidado y Uso de Animales de Laboratorio (CICUAL) of the Facultad de Ciencias de la Salud, Universidad Nacional de Salta (Salta, Argentina). The study was approved under Resolution CD No. 093-22 (Expedient No. 12.092/21), issued on 4 April 2022.

### 2.2. Immunization Protocol

Mice (n = 7; 3 females and 4 males) were immunized subcutaneously with three doses of 20 µg of N-Tc52/TSKb20 combined with 15 μg of the QuilA adjuvant (InvivoGen, Toulouse, France), administrated in 50 µL injections every 3 weeks. A non-vaccinated control group received 15 μg of QuilA alone (n = 6; 3 females and 3 males) and was included throughout the study. On day 170 post-vaccination, animals were euthanized following ethical standards to assess humoral and cellular responses.

### 2.3. Detection of N-Tc52/TSKb20-Specific Antibodies

For antibody determination assays, serum samples were collected from vaccinated and non-vaccinated mice at 170 days after the final dose. Sera were obtained by blood centrifugation at 3500 rpm, which were subsequently stored at −20 °C until IgG1 and IgG2c evaluation; 96-well plates were coated with 0.25 μg/well of the chimeric protein in 100 µL of Coating Buffer and incubated overnight at 4 °C. IgG1 and IgG2c subclasses were determined by ELISA. Plates were blocked with 5% skim milk in PBS for 1 h at 37 °C and then incubated with sera diluted 1:20 (100 μL/well) for 1 h at 37 °C. Biotinylated anti-IgG1 or anti-IgG2c antibodies (BD Biosciences, San José, CA, USA) were added at dilutions of 1:4000 and 1:2000, respectively, and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C. Horseradish peroxidase-conjugated streptavidin (1:7500) was subsequently added and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C. Signal development was performed with 1 mg/mL of o-Phenylenediamine dihydrochloride OPD (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) with a dilution 1:10 of 30% p/v H2O2 30% for 20 min and stopped with 2 N H2SO4. Optical density was measured at 492 nm using a TECAN Infinite F50 plate reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA).

### 2.4. Cell Culture-Derived Trypomastigote and Trypanolytic Activity

Cell culture-derived trypomastigotes of the Tulahuen strain (DTU VI) were obtained as follows. Epimastigotes were maintained in vitro through routine passages and cultured at 28 °C in Liver Infusion Tryptose (LIT) medium supplemented with 20 µg/mL hemin (Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA), 100 IU/mL penicillin, 100 µg/mL streptomycin, and 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum at 56 °C for 1 h (FBS; Natocor, Córdoba, Argentina). To induce differentiation into metacyclic trypomastigotes, cultures were subjected to nutrient starvation for 3 weeks without medium supplementation, followed by overnight incubation at 37 °C. Metacyclic trypomastigotes were collected by centrifugation at 1500 rpm for 10 min, washed twice with PBS, and used to infect L929 cells at 60% confluence. Infected cells were cultured in DMEM at 37 °C with 5% CO2 for 15 days, during which cell culture-derived trypomastigotes were released into the media. Trypomastigotes were then collected by centrifugation, washed, and used to assess antibody-mediated parasite lysis.

To evaluate trypanolytic activity, sera from vaccinated and non-vaccinated mice were heat-inactivated at 56 °C 30 min to abolish endogenous complement activity. Subsequently, 40 µL of serum was mixed with 2 × 105 cell culture-derived trypomastigote and 40 µL of human serum diluted 1:2 as an exogenous complement source, then incubated 3 h at 37 °C. Under these conditions, the assay specifically assessed the capacity of vaccine-induced antibodies to promote lysis of T. cruzi trypomastigotes in the presence of active human complement. The percentage of trypomastigote lysis was determined by counting live parasites in 1:10 diluted samples using a Neubauer chamber (Boeco, Hamburg, Germany) under light microscopy at 1 and 3 h post-incubation. All measurements were performed in duplicate.

### 2.5. Splenocyte Culture

Spleens were harvested from euthanized mice on day 170 post-vaccination and placed on 15 mL tubes containing Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI 1640) medium supplemented with L-glutamine (Biological Industries, Beit Haemek, Israel). Spleens were then gently macerated through a sterile mesh on ice, and the resulting cell suspension was collected by centrifugation at 160× g at 4 °C for 10 min. Erythrocytes were removed by resuspending the pellet in lysis solution (0.17 M Tris, 0.16 M NH4Cl, pH 7.2). The remaining splenocytes were washed and resuspended in RPMI supplemented with 10% FBS that was heat-inactivated. Cell number and viability were assessed by Trypan blue exclusion using a Neubauer chamber.

### 2.6. Tulahuen HP Preparation

A total soluble protein homogenate from T. cruzi Tulahuen strain (Tulahuen HP) was prepared from a culture of 1 × 109 epimastigotes in the exponential growth phase. Parasites were maintained in LIT medium supplemented with 20 µg/mL hemin, 100 IU/mL penicillin, 100 µg/mL streptomycin, and 10% heat-inactivated FBS at 56 °C for 1 h. Parasites were then centrifuged at 1000× g, washed, and resuspended in a lysis buffer (100 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, pH 8). The suspension was incubated at 4 °C for 10 min. Parasite lysis was completed by three freeze–thaw cycles followed by sonication (three pulses of 1 min at 40 W, 80% amplitude) and confirmed by microscopic observation. The lysate was then centrifuged at 20,000× g at 4 °C for 20 min. The supernatant containing soluble parasite proteins was collected and sterilized by filtration through a 0.22 µm membrane. Protein homogenates were stored at −70 °C until use.

### 2.7. Activation-Induced Marker Assay (AIM)

The frequency and activation of specific CD8+ and CD4+ T cells were evaluated using an activation-induced marker (AIM) assay in splenocytes obtained at 170 days post-vaccination [42,44]. Splenocytes (1 × 106 cells/well) were stimulated for 15 h with 0.2 μM of the chimeric protein, 0.4 μM of the TSKb20 synthetic peptide (GenScript, Piscataway, NJ, USA) or 15 μg/mL of Tulahuen HP. Unstimulated cells (culture medium) served as negative controls, and cells stimulated with Concanavalin A (CoA, 5 μg/mL, Merck) were used as positive controls. After incubation, cells were washed with PBS and stained with anti- IA/IE-APCCy7 (clone m5/114.15.2), anti-B220-APCCy7 (clone RA3-6B2) y Zombie Fixable Viability near-IR dye (exclusion/DUMP panel), followed by anti-CD8-PerCP (clone 53-6.7), anti-CD4-FITC (clone GK15), anti-CD25-APC (clone PC61) and anti-CD69-PECy7 (clone H1.2F3) (Biolegend, San Diego, CA, USA) for 30 min at 4 °C in the dark. Cells were then fixed with 4% formaldehyde for 16 h at 4 °C, washed with PBS and acquired on a BD FACS Canto II cytometer. Data were analyzed using FlowJo vX.0.7.

### 2.8. Cytokine Quantification

Supernatants from splenocyte cultures (1 × 106 cells/mL), collected after 15 h of stimulation with 0.2 μM N-Tc52/TSKb20, 0.4 μM TSKb20 peptide or 15 μg/mL Tulahuen HP, were used to measure TNF-α and IL-10 levels using the Mouse cytokine ELISA MAX™ Standard Set (BioLegend) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, plates were coated overnight with capture antibody (1:200), blocked with 10% FBS, and incubated for 2 h with the samples. Detection antibody (1:200) was added and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. After washes, horseradish peroxidase (1:1000) was added and incubated for 30 min. Signal development was performed for 30 min with 1 mg/mL OPD and 1:10 diluted 30% H2O2, and the reaction was stopped with 2 N H2SO4. Absorbance was read at 492 nm using a TECAN plate reader. The limits of detection of the assays were 7.8 pg/mL and 31.3 pg/mL for TNF-α and IL-10, respectively.

### 2.9. ELISPOT Assay for IFN-γ Detection

An ELISPOT assay (BD Biosciences) was performed to quantify IFN-γ-producing splenocytes from mice euthanized 170 days post-vaccination, following the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, ELISPOT plates were coated overnight with anti-IFN-γ capture antibody and blocked for 2 h at room temperature. Splenocytes (1 × 106 cells/well) were seeded and stimulated with 0.2 μM N-Tc52/TSKb20 protein, 0.4 μM TSKb20 peptide, or 15 μg/mL Tulahuen HP for 24 h at 37 °C with 5% CO2. After incubation, plates were washed and incubated with a biotinylated anti-IFN-γ detection antibody, followed by streptavidin–horseradish peroxidase. Spots were developed using 3,3′-diaminobenzidine tetrahydrochloride (DAB; Merck) and 1:10 diluted 30% H2O2. IFN-γ-secreting cells were quantified using an ImmunoSpot S5.0.3 reader at the Instituto Fatala Chabén, Buenos Aires, Argentina. Unstimulated cells (culture medium) served as negative controls, and cells stimulated with CoA (5 μg/mL; Merck) were used as positive controls.

### 2.10. Identification of Specific Immunological Memory Subpopulations

To characterize antigen-specific CD4+ and CD8+ memory T-cell populations, spleens were collected 170 days post-vaccination and processed for flow cytometry analysis. Splenocytes (1 × 106 cells/well) were stimulated for 15 h with 0.2 μM of the chimeric protein, 0.4 μM of the TSKb20 peptide, or 15 μg/mL of Tulahuen HP. Unstimulated cells (culture medium) served as negative controls, and cells stimulated with CoA (5 μg/mL; Merck) were used as positive controls. Following incubation, cells were washed with PBS and stained with anti-IA/IE-APCCy7 (clone m5/114.15.2), anti-B220-APCCy7 (clone RA3-6B2) and Zombie Fixable Viability near-IR dye (exclusion/DUMP panel), followed by anti-CD8-PerCP (clone 53-6.7), anti-CD4-FITC (clone GK15), anti-CD62L-APC (clone MEL-14) and anti-CD44-PECy7 (clone IM7) (Biolegend) for 30 min at 4 °C in the dark. Cells were then fixed with 4% formaldehyde for 16 h at 4 °C, washed with PBS, and acquired on a BD FACS Canto II cytometer. Data were analyzed using FlowJo vX.0.7.

### 2.11. Statistical Analysis

Data distribution was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk normality test prior to statistical analysis. Data were then analyzed using two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Sidak’s multiple-comparisons test. Results are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 8.0.2 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). Differences were considered statistically significant when p < 0.05.

## 3. Results

### 3.1. N-Tc52/TSKb20 Vaccination Induces Durable IgG2c-Biased Antibody Responses with Trypanolytic Activity

To evaluate the humoral immune response, female and male C57BL/6 mice were immunized following the vaccination protocol described in Figure 1A. Antigen-specific IgG1 and IgG2c levels were measured 170 days after the final immunization. Two-way ANOVA analysis revealed no significant interaction between sex and vaccination, indicating that the effect of vaccination on the humoral response was independent of sex. Accordingly, data from both sexes were analyzed together. Mice vaccinated with N-Tc52/TSKb20 exhibited significant levels of antigen-specific IgG2c antibodies against the chimeric protein, whereas IgG1 levels were undetectable (p < 0.05) (Figure 1B). The level of this isotype was significantly higher in vaccinated animals compared with non-vaccinated controls (p < 0.05) (Figure 1B). This profile was indicative of a sustained Th1-oriented humoral response. Notably, persistent IgG2c antibodies were detected in four vaccinated mice (two females and two males), highlighting inter-individual differences in the long-term humoral response.

We next assessed the functional capacity of immune sera to mediate in vitro trypomastigote lysis. As shown in Figure 1C, after 1 h of incubation, sera from vaccinated mice displayed significantly higher lytic activity than non-immune sera, with approximately 20% parasite lysis observed in nearly half of the samples (p < 0.05). The frequencies of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and their activated subpopulations (CD25+CD69+) were determined by flow cytometry following the gating strategy shown in Figure 2A.

We first assessed whether changes in CD4+ and CD8+ T cell frequencies upon antigen recall were influenced by sex. Two-way ANOVA revealed a significant interaction between sex and vaccination when cells were stimulated with TSKb20 (p < 0.05) and Tulahuen HP (p < 0.01) for both CD4+ and CD8+ T cell populations. Therefore, subsequent analyses of T cell frequencies were performed separately for females and males. In male mice (filled circles), Tulahuen HP stimulation induced a shift in T cell subset distribution, characterized by a decreased frequency of CD4+ T cells (Figure 2B, left panel) and a concomitant increase in CD8+ T cells (Figure 2B, right panel) in vaccinated animals relative to non-vaccinated controls (p < 0.001). No significant differences were observed with the other stimuli. In contrast, the most evident differences in female mice (open circles) were observed following stimulation with the TSKb20 peptide. Vaccinated females exhibited an increased frequency of CD4+ T cell accompanied by a reduction in CD8+ T cells compared with non-vaccinated controls (p < 0.05) (Figure 2B), revealing a trend opposite to that observed in males following Tulahuen HP stimulation. No differences were detected in females with the remaining stimuli.

Antigen-specific T cell activation was subsequently assessed by measuring the co-expression of CD25 and CD69. Unlike the population frequency data, no significant interaction between sex and vaccination was detected in activated T cell subsets, indicating that the vaccine-induced activation response was not influenced by sex. Therefore, data from female and male mice were combined for further analysis. A consistent trend toward higher frequencies of activated CD4+CD25+CD69+ T cells was observed in vaccinated animals compared with non-vaccinated, irrespective of the antigen used for re-stimulation. This effect was particularly evident following stimulation with the TSKb20 peptide (p < 0.05) (Figure 2C, left panel). Importantly, within the CD8+CD25+CD69+ subpopulation, re-stimulation with the TSKb20 peptide elicited a significant increase in splenocytes from N-Tc52/TSKb20-vaccinated mice compared with the non-vaccinated group (p < 0.01) (Figure 2C, right panel), highlighting the persistence of antigen-specific CD8+ T cell responsiveness. Although no significant increase was detected following stimulation with the full N-Tc52/TSKb20 protein or Tulahuen HP, these findings collectively support the long-term maintenance of functional antigen-specific cellular immunity induced by vaccination.

TNF-α production was not influenced by sex, as no significant interaction between sex and vaccination was detected. Therefore, data from male and female mice were analyzed together. Vaccinated mice exhibited increased TNF-α production compared to non-vaccinated upon re-stimulation with the TSKb20 peptide (p < 0.01). In contrast, no differences in TNF-α levels were observed following stimulation with the full N-Tc52/TSKb20 protein or Tulahuen HP (Figure 3A).

### 3.4. Induction of Specific CD4+ and CD8+ T Cell Memory Subpopulations by N-Tc52/TSKb20 Vaccination

The frequencies of CD4+ and CD8+ naïve (TN: CD62L+CD44−), central memory (TCM: CD62L+CD44+), and effector memory (TEM: CD62L−CD44+) T cell populations were analyzed by flow cytometry in splenocytes obtained, using the gating strategy depicted in Figure 4A. Splenocytes were re-stimulated in vitro with the N-Tc52/TSKb20 chimeric protein, the TSKb20 peptide, or the Tulahuen HP. No sex-related differences were observed in the CD4+ memory T cell subsets. The frequency of the CD4+ naïve subpopulation remained largely stable across conditions. However, following stimulation with Tulahuen HP, vaccinated animals displayed a significant reduction in TN subset compared with non-vaccinated controls (64% vs. 77% respectively; p < 0.01) (Figure 4B). Regarding the CD4+ memory compartment, vaccinated animals presented a significant higher proportion of TCM cells following stimulation with the T. cruzi protein homogenate compared with non-vaccinated animals (2.5% vs. 1.06% respectively; p < 0.05) (Figure 4C). Likewise, stimulation with the TSKb20 peptide or Tulahuen HP resulted in increased frequencies of CD4+ TEM cells in vaccinated mice relative to non-vaccinated controls (4.3% vs. 2.4%, p < 0.01, and 4.7% vs. 2.6%, p < 0.05, respectively) (Figure 4D). Overall, the relative distribution of the average percentages of CD4+ T cell subpopulations was compared between non-vaccinated and vaccinated groups following re-stimulation with Tulahuen HP. As shown in Figure 4E, vaccinated animals exhibited a lower proportion of CD4+ TN cells compared to non-vaccinated mice (90.4% vs. 94.4% respectively), a greater proportion of CD4+ TCM cells (3.4% vs. 1.4%) and a higher frequency of CD4+ TEM cells (6.1% vs. 3.2%) (Figure 4E).
